### 2
Your first job is about learning how to contribute, not proving you already know everything.

- Ask questions early. Explain what you’ve tried and where you’re stuck so others can help effectively.
- Read existing code before changing it. Learn the team’s patterns, tools, and reasons behind decisions.
- Keep changes small. They’re easier to review, test, and debug.
- Treat code reviews as collaboration, not a judgment of your ability.
- Communicate progress and blockers. A timely heads-up matters more than silently struggling.
- Keep notes and protect your downtime. Steady learning beats trying to master everything at once.

### 3
Sunlight looks white, but it’s actually a mix of many colors. When it enters Earth’s atmosphere, it bumps into tiny gas molecules that scatter the light in different directions.

Blue light scatters much more strongly than red light, so blue light reaches your eyes from all across the sky—not just from the direction of the Sun. Violet scatters even more, but our eyes are less sensitive to it, and sunlight contains less violet than blue, so the sky looks blue.

At sunset, sunlight travels through more atmosphere before reaching you. Much of the blue light gets scattered away, leaving the reds and oranges you see near the Sun.

### 2
Your first job is about learning how to contribute, not proving you already know everything.

- Ask questions early. Explain what you’ve tried and where you’re stuck so others can help effectively.
- Read existing code before changing it. Learn the team’s patterns, tools, and reasons behind decisions.
- Keep changes small. They’re easier to review, test, and debug.
- Treat code reviews as collaboration, not a judgment of your ability.
- Communicate progress and blockers. A timely heads-up matters more than silently struggling.
- Keep notes and protect your downtime. Steady learning beats trying to master everything at once.

### 3
Sunlight looks white, but it’s actually a mix of many colors. When it enters Earth’s atmosphere, it bumps into tiny gas molecules that scatter the light in different directions.

Blue light scatters much more strongly than red light, so blue light reaches your eyes from all across the sky—not just from the direction of the Sun. Violet scatters even more, but our eyes are less sensitive to it, and sunlight contains less violet than blue, so the sky looks blue.

At sunset, sunlight travels through more atmosphere before reaching you. Much of the blue light gets scattered away, leaving the reds and oranges you see near the Sun.
